facts.text: North Bay emerged as a post village in the mid‑19th century, founded by families such as the Halsteads, Cooks, and Graves drawn to Oneida Lake’s water power.
North Bay’s climate is humid continental (Dfb), with January lows around 13°F and July highs near 81°F, and about 47 inches of evenly spread precipitation.
Before European contact, the Oneida called the lake Tsioqui, meaning “white water,” and used the area for hunting, fishing, and seasonal villages.
The Treaty of Fort Stanwix in 1788 allowed New York State to negotiate directly with the Oneida, leading to land cessions that opened central New York to settlers.
Oneida Lake, adjacent to North Bay, averages 22.3 feet deep, has a shoreline over 77 miles, and supports wetlands, small streams, and a productive freshwater ecosystem.
